edges.description: Spirochetes that cross the barrier rapidly seed the bloodstream and visceral organs.
Organ dissemination brings leptospires into proximity with vascular endothelium and activates pathogenic host inflammatory responses.
Systemic leptospiremic infection manifests as an acute high-fever illness.
Kidney seeding produces a proximal-tubule-centered lesion that disrupts sodium and water transport.
Liver seeding produces a hepatocellular lesion that disrupts tissue architecture and bile handling.
Hepatic parenchymal disruption contributes to the jaundice branch of severe icteric leptospirosis.
Loss of pulmonary endothelial integrity contributes to leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome.
Systemic vascular leakage contributes to the hemorrhagic and pulmonary branch of severe icteric leptospirosis.
Proximal tubular injury and transporter loss manifest clinically as leptospiral acute kidney injury.
Kidney injury joins hepatic and pulmonary involvement in the multi-organ syndrome of Weil's disease.
Hepatic involvement manifests as severe icteric leptospirosis.
Renal involvement manifests as acute kidney injury.
Pulmonary vascular injury manifests as pulmonary hemorrhage.
Cardiac involvement in severe leptospirosis manifests as myocarditis.

nodes.description: Acute kidney injury is a defining severe manifestation of Weil's disease and is frequent in ICU-level severe leptospirosis.

evidence.reference_title: Severe leptospirosis in the intensive care unit: single centre prospective cohort study from Sri Lanka.
evidence.snippet: Among them, 99.1% (n = 115) developed acute kidney injury, 62.1% (n = 72) developed pulmonary haemorrhage, and 75.9% (n = 88) developed myocarditis.

nodes.description: Leptospira-associated capillary injury is amplified by cytokine release, adhesion-molecule upregulation, and complement activation, disrupting endothelial integrity and promoting vascular leakage.

evidence.reference_title: Leptospirosis-associated pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome: immune mechanisms, clinical manifestations, and experimental models.
evidence.snippet: the host immune response, via the cytokine release, high expression of adhesion molecules, and activation of the Complement System, may further disrupt endothelial integrity, promoting vascular leakage

nodes.description: Pathogenic Leptospira enter the human host through mucosa or abraded skin after animal-contact or urine-contaminated environmental exposure.

evidence.snippet: Human infections are primarily acquired through direct or indirect contact with water or soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals.

nodes.description: Invasive Leptospira disseminate through blood and seed the liver, lungs, and kidneys early in systemic infection.

evidence.reference_title: Establishment of a leptospirosis model in guinea pigs using an epicutaneous inoculations route.
evidence.snippet: In the guinea pigs with abraded skin inoculations, leptospires were detected in blood as early as 2 h post infection (p.i.) and then disseminated to the liver, lungs and kidneys of almost all animals within 96 h p.i..

nodes.description: Severe L. interrogans infection can dissociate hepatocytes and disrupt liver parenchymal architecture, a hepatic branch that contributes to the icteric component of Weil's disease.

evidence.reference_title: Leptospira interrogans serovar Copenhageni infection and exudative glomerulonephritis in rehabilitated gray seals (Halichoerus grypus) and harbor seals (Phoca vitulina) in Ireland.
evidence.snippet: Common histological findings were acute renal tubular necrosis, exudative glomerulonephritis (GN), hepatocyte dissociation and pulmonary hemorrhage.

nodes.description: High fever is part of the acute severe Weil's disease presentation.

evidence.snippet: The disease ranges from a mild, self-limiting illness known as Akiyami to severe Weil's disease, which presents with high fever; jaundice; hemorrhagic tendencies involving the skin, nasal cavity, and lungs; and acute renal failure.

nodes.description: Severe leptospiral vascular and parenchymal injury converges on kidney, liver, and lung, producing the jaundice, acute kidney injury, pulmonary hemorrhage, and multi-organ dysfunction that define Weil's disease.

nodes.description: Doxycycline is used for mild-to-moderate leptospirosis, while severe leptospirosis, including Weil's disease, is treated with penicillin-class or third-generation cephalosporin antibacterial therapy; randomized-trial evidence for mortality reduction remains very uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Treatment typically involves doxycycline for mild-to-moderate cases, whereas penicillin is recommended for severe diseases.

evidence.reference_title: Efficacy and safety of antibiotics for treatment of leptospirosis: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
evidence.snippet: Six antibiotics resulted in significantly shorter defervescence times compared to the control, namely cefotaxime (MD, - 1.88; 95% CI = - 2.60 to - 1.15), azithromycin (MD, - 1.74; 95% CI = - 2.52 to - 0.95), doxycycline (MD, - 1.53; 95% CI = - 2.05 to - 1.00), ceftriaxone (MD, - 1.22; 95% CI = - 1.89 to - 0.55), penicillin (MD, - 1.22; 95% CI = - 1.80 to - 0.64), and penicillin or ampicillin (MD, - 0.08; 95% CI = - 1.01 to - 0.59).
As the certainty of evidence is very low, we do not know if antibiotics provide little to no effect on all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, or adverse events considered non-serious.
